name: When Not to Use AI
title: When Not to Use AI
answer: Some teaching moments should stay entirely with the teacher, including personal conversations with students, feedback on deeply personal writing, and decisions about grades or placement. AI is also a poor fit when accuracy matters and the teacher cannot easily check the output, or when a task is worth doing slowly because it carries meaning. The idea matters because using AI in these moments can make students feel processed rather than seen, and it can introduce errors a teacher is not equipped to catch.

sections.body: This idea sets out the boundaries of AI use in teaching rather than its possibilities. It identifies three situations where a teacher's own attention and voice should not be replaced: moments that are personal, moments where accuracy is critical and hard to verify, and moments whose slowness is part of their value. The problem it solves is the assumption that every task should be handed to AI or made faster. It gives teachers permission to decide for themselves when AI helps and when it does not.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher keeps certain conversations and written responses in their own hands, such as talking with a student about a struggle, commenting on personal writing, or making a call about a grade or placement. When a teacher is unfamiliar with a topic, the safer route is trusted curriculum materials or a colleague's expertise rather than an AI draft the teacher cannot properly check. The text does not divide this guidance by grade band, so it applies the same way across year groups. AI is described as working best when the teacher knows the subject well enough to catch its mistakes. Teachers are also free to keep some tasks slow, such as writing a careful note to a struggling student or planning a lesson they care about.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice and professional judgement rather than research, and the book presents it as guidance drawn from teaching experience. No evidence label is attached to the claims about when AI should be avoided.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the nature of the task and by the teacher's own knowledge. Personal conversations, feedback on deeply personal writing, and decisions about grades or placement stay with a person because AI there can make students feel processed rather than seen. Where accuracy is critical and checking is hard, the decision to use trusted materials or a colleague instead of AI stays with the teacher. The choice of when AI helps and when it does not also remains a human decision, and the text treats the value of doing some tasks slowly as a reason to keep them that way.
